Section 3 • Transmitted Flux

3.4 Optical Depth Along the Line of Sight

The previous subsection defines the local absorption produced by the gas at a given point along the photon trajectory. We now turn this local description into a cumulative one. The optical depth is obtained by integrating the absorption encountered by the photon along its full path, and therefore measures the total attenuation produced by the intervening inhomogeneous gas distribution between emission and observation.

In full generality, the photon propagates along a null geodesic \(\gamma\), which need not be a straight line in comoving space. The optical depth produced by transition \(j\) of species \(i\) is then written as a path integral along that trajectory: \begin{align} \tau_{ij}(\vec{x}_{\perp}, \Lambda) = \mathcal{C}_j \int_{\gamma} \frac{ n_{i\,\mathrm{com}}\!\left(\vec{x}\right) }{ a(\vec{x})^{3} } \; \phi_{ij}\!\left(\vec{x},\Lambda\right) \; dl_{\mathrm{phys}}, \tag{3.17} \end{align} where \begin{align} \mathcal{C}_j \equiv \frac{e^{2}f_j}{4\varepsilon_{0}m_e c}. \tag{3.18} \end{align}

This expression has a simple interpretation: at each point along the trajectory, the local contribution to the optical depth is given by the proper number density of absorbers, \( n_{i\,\mathrm{phys}}(\vec{x}) = n_{i\,\mathrm{com}}(\vec{x})/a(\vec{x})^{3}, \) multiplied by the local line profile and by the proper line element \(dl_{\mathrm{phys}}\).

In many practical applications, however, the photon trajectories can be approximated as straight lines in comoving space. In that case, it is convenient to decompose the comoving position as \begin{align} \vec{x} = (\vec{x}_{\perp},x_{\parallel}), \tag{3.19} \end{align} where \(\vec{x}_{\perp}\) labels the transverse comoving position of the sightline and \(x_{\parallel}\) parametrizes the propagation along it. For a fixed sightline \(\vec{x}_{\perp}\), the optical depth becomes \begin{align} \tau_{ij}\!\left(\vec{x}_{\perp},\Lambda\right) = \mathcal{C}_j \int_{x_{\parallel,\mathrm{em}}}^{x_{\parallel,\mathrm{f}}} \frac{ n_{i\,\mathrm{com}}\!\left(\vec{x}_{\perp},x'_{\parallel}\right) }{ a\!\left(\vec{x}_{\perp},x'_{\parallel}\right)^{3} } \; \phi_{ij}\!\left(\vec{x}_{\perp},x'_{\parallel},\Lambda\right) \; a\!\left(\vec{x}_{\perp},x'_{\parallel}\right)\, dx'_{\parallel}, \tag{3.20} \end{align} where we used \begin{align} dl_{\mathrm{phys}} = a\,dx_{\parallel}. \tag{3.21} \end{align}

Therefore, Eq. (3.20) should be understood as the straight-line approximation to the more general path-integral expression in Eq. (3.17). This form is particularly convenient in practice, since it makes explicit that the optical depth may vary from one sightline to another through its dependence on the transverse position \(\vec{x}_{\perp}\).

Finally, if several transitions contribute to the absorption, the total optical depth is obtained by summing the individual contributions: \begin{align} \tau\!\left(\vec{x}_{\perp},\Lambda\right) = \sum_{\{i,j\}} \tau_{ij}\!\left(\vec{x}_{\perp},\Lambda\right). \tag{3.22} \end{align}
